nes.description: The NES revolutionized the video game industry after the 1983 crash, setting quality standards and introducing iconic franchises like Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, and Metroid.

fds.description: Peripheral for the Famicom (Japanese NES) that used proprietary floppy disks, allowing for larger games, game saves, and an improved additional sound channel.

snes.description: The successor to the NES that introduced 16-bit graphics, the Mode 7 chip for pseudo-3D effects and some of the best games in history like Super Mario World, A Link to the Past and Super Metroid.

snes-msu1.description: Virtual chip for SNES that allows CD-quality audio and FMV video. Used in hacks and new games to drastically improve the console's multimedia experience.

satellaview.description: Satellite modem for SNES released in Japan. It allowed downloading games and content through satellite radio broadcasts, including exclusive Zelda and Mario titles.

sufami.description: Adapter for SNES manufactured by Bandai that used mini-cartridges. It allowed the use of two cartridges simultaneously to exchange data between compatible games.

n64.description: Nintendo's first console to offer true 3D graphics. Famous for innovative titles like Super Mario 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and GoldenEye 007. It used cartridges instead of CDs.

gamecube.description: A compact console with a distinctive design and ergonomic controllers. It stood out for its powerful hardware and excellent first-party games like Super Smash Bros. Melee, Metroid Prime, and The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker.

wii.description: Revolutionized gaming with motion controls, making it accessible to the whole family. Its library includes Wii Sports, Super Mario Galaxy, and The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess.

wiiu.description: Introduced the innovative GamePad with a touch screen, allowing for asymmetric and off-TV play. Home to exceptional titles like Super Mario 3D World, Splatoon, and The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

switch.description: A hybrid console that functions as both a handheld and a home console. It has been a massive success with games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, Animal Crossing: New Horizons, and Super Mario Odyssey.

gb.description: The handheld that defined mobile gaming. Its long battery life and library of classic games like Tetris, Pokémon, and Super Mario Land turned it into a cultural phenomenon.

gbc.description: An evolution of the Game Boy with a color screen. Compatible with original Game Boy games and featuring its own library including Pokémon Crystal and The Legend of Zelda: Oracle series.

gba.description: A 32-bit handheld with capabilities similar to the SNES. Its catalog includes masterpieces like Advance Wars, Metroid Fusion, and remakes of NES and SNES classics.

nds.description: A revolutionary console with dual screens and touch capabilities. It introduced innovative ways to play with titles like Brain Age, Nintendogs, and New Super Mario Bros.
nds.cpu: ARM946E-S at 67 MHz + ARM7TDMI at 33 MHz

3ds.description: First handheld console with glasses-free stereoscopic 3D. Large library with games like Pokémon X/Y, Super Mario 3D Land, and The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds.

virtualboy.description: Famous Nintendo console that promised to immerse the player in virtual reality through monochromatic stereoscopic graphics (red and black). It was a commercial failure due to discomfort.

genesis.description: The console that challenged Nintendo in the 90s with its 'cool' attitude and Sonic the Hedgehog. Home to classics like Streets of Rage, Golden Axe and Phantasy Star.

megadrive.description: Original name in Japan and Europe for Sega's 16-bit console. Identical to the American Genesis, it was a massive success capable of rivaling the Super Nintendo.

megadrive-msu.description: Virtual expansion for Mega Drive that allows adding high-fidelity soundtracks and FMV video to games, similar to the SNES MSU-1.

segacd.description: A CD-ROM expansion for the Mega Drive that allowed for enhanced graphics, CD-quality audio, and FMV animations. It stood out for games like Sonic CD and Snatcher.

sega32x.description: A 32-bit expansion for the Genesis that significantly improved graphics. Despite its short lifespan, it offered notable ports like Doom and Virtua Fighter.

saturn.description: 32-bit console known for its excellent library of 2D games and arcade ports. Notable titles include Panzer Dragoon Saga, Nights into Dreams, and Virtua Fighter 2.

segastv.description: Arcade board based entirely on the Sega Saturn architecture, allowing for perfect conversions between arcades and the home console.

dreamcast.description: Sega's last console and the first with a built-in modem. Ahead of its time with innovative games like Shenmue, Jet Set Radio, and Phantasy Star Online.

gamegear.description: Color handheld that competed with Game Boy. Backlit screen and quality game library, but with shorter battery life. Noted for Sonic and Shinobi.

mastersystem.description: Sega's 8-bit console that competed directly with the NES. Although it had less global success, it was immensely popular in Europe and Brazil, noted for games like Alex Kidd and Sonic.

sg1000.description: Sega's first home video game console. Released on the same day as Nintendo's Famicom in Japan, it laid the groundwork for what would later become the Master System.

psx.description: The console that brought Sony into the video game market and popularized CD-ROMs. Massive library with classics like Final Fantasy VII, Metal Gear Solid, and Crash Bandicoot.

ps2.description: The best-selling console in history. Built-in DVD player and an incomparable library with titles like God of War, Shadow of the Colossus, and Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas.

ps3.description: A powerful console with the Cell Processor and Blu-ray. It introduced the PlayStation Network and trophies. Standouts include The Last of Us, Uncharted series, and God of War III.

ps4.description: A gaming-focused console with x86 architecture. Great success with exclusives like Bloodborne, Spider-Man, Horizon Zero Dawn, and God of War (2018).

ps5.description: New generation console with ultra-fast SSD, ray tracing, and the innovative DualSense with haptic feedback. Standout games include Demon's Souls Remake and Returnal.

psp.description: A multimedia handheld with a wide screen and advanced multimedia capabilities. Quality library including God of War: Chains of Olympus, Monster Hunter, and Lumines.

psvita.description: Successor to the PSP with a touch OLED screen and a rear touchpad. Despite its shorter commercial life, it cultivated a dedicated fan base with titles like Persona 4 Golden and Uncharted: Golden Abyss.

xbox.description: Microsoft's first foray into consoles with powerful hardware based on PC technology. It introduced Xbox Live and Halo: Combat Evolved, which revolutionized console FPS games.

xbox360.description: Perfected online gaming with an improved Xbox Live and achievement system. Exceptional library with Halo 3, Gears of War, and Mass Effect.

xboxone.description: An all-in-one multimedia console with an entertainment focus. It stood out for its backward compatibility and services like Xbox Game Pass. Key titles include Forza Horizon series and Halo 5.
xboxone.resolution: Up to 1080p (4K on Xbox One X)

xboxseriesx.description: New generation consoles focused on performance and speed. Series X offers native 4K and ray tracing, while Series S is more compact and affordable. Both include Quick Resume and Game Pass.
xboxseriesx.resolution: Up to 4K (8K supported on Series X)

atari2600.description: One of the first successful consoles with interchangeable cartridges. Popularized arcade classics at home like Space Invaders, Pac-Man, and Pitfall!

vectrex.description: A unique console that included its own vector monitor. Unlike other consoles that used pixels, the Vectrex drew smooth lines, offering a unique arcade aesthetic at home.

atari5200.description: Successor to the 2600 with better graphics and sound. Based on the Atari 8-bit computer hardware. Notable for its arcade ports and analog controllers.

atari7800.description: A console backward compatible with the Atari 2600, designed to compete with the NES. It significantly improved graphics and offered excellent versions of arcade games.

atarilynx.description: First color handheld console with a backlit screen. Technically superior to Game Boy but with less commercial success. Noted for its multiplayer gaming capability.

lynx.description: First color handheld console with a backlit screen. Technically superior to Game Boy but with less commercial success. Noted for its multiplayer gaming capability.

atarijaguar.description: Self-proclaimed as the first 64-bit console. Atari's final console had a limited library but includes cult titles like Tempest 2000 and Alien vs Predator.

colecovision.description: A console that stood out for its excellent arcade game adaptations. Offered superior graphics compared to its competitors of the time like Donkey Kong and Zaxxon.

o2.description: Successor to the first console in history. It included a full keyboard on the main unit and stood out for its speech synthesis and strategy games.

intellivision.description: The first 16-bit console that rivaled the Atari 2600. Innovative controller with a numeric keypad and directional disc. Diverse library of sports and strategy games.

neogeo.description: Identical arcade and home arcade system hardware. Known for its high-quality fighting and run-and-gun games like Metal Slug, The King of Fighters, and Samurai Shodown.

neogeocd.description: A more affordable version of the Neo Geo that used CDs. Same games but with long load times. Popular for making expensive Neo Geo games accessible.

ngp.description: SNK's handheld with a monochrome screen. Notable for its excellent analog stick and handheld versions of Neo Geo franchises.

ngpc.description: Color version of the NGP with excellent fighting and puzzle games. Backward compatible with the NGP. Despite its quality, it couldn't compete with the Game Boy Color.

wonderswan.description: Japanese handheld designed by the creator of the Game Boy. Notable for its low battery consumption and library of JRPGs. Popular in Japan but never released internationally.

wonderswancolor.description: Color version of the WonderSwan backward compatible with original games. Quality library including Final Fantasy and ports of classic games.

pokemini.description: The smallest console with interchangeable cartridges in the world. Included vibration and motion sensors, focusing exclusively on the Pokémon franchise.

playdia.description: A CD-based 8-bit console that used an infrared controller. It was aimed at a young audience and focused on interactive software and anime, such as Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon.

pippin.description: Multimedia platform designed by Apple and manufactured primarily by Bandai. Based on Macintosh architecture, it tried to be a mix between a computer and a console, but its high price limited its success.

pcengine.description: An 8-bit console with a 16-bit graphics chip that rivaled the Mega Drive in Japan. Excellent library of shoot 'em ups and RPGs. Great success in Japan but limited in the West.

pcenginecd.description: The first successful CD-ROM expansion for consoles. Allowed for CD-quality audio and improved graphics. Highlight library with Ys series and Castlevania: Rondo of Blood.

supervision.description: A monochrome handheld console released as a budget alternative to the Game Boy. It had a larger screen but a more limited and lower-quality game library.

pcfx.description: Successor to the PC Engine focused on anime and FMV. Never released outside Japan. Small but cult library, mainly visual novels and anime games.

x68000.description: A powerful Japanese workstation famous for its 'perfect ports' of Capcom and Konami arcade games. Extremely advanced hardware for its time.

3do.description: Ambitious multimedia console with advanced technology but a prohibitive price. Standout for innovative games like Gex, Road Rash, and the original The Need for Speed.

cdi.description: An interactive multimedia system remembered primarily for its infamous licensed Zelda and Mario games. Focused more on education and multimedia than pure gaming.

amiga1200.description: The most advanced home model in the Amiga line. With the AGA chipset, it allowed for much higher graphical power, capable of showing up to 256 simultaneous colors from a palette of 16.8 million.

amiga500.description: The most popular model in the Amiga family. It revolutionized the home market with its impressive sound and graphics capabilities for the time, becoming the standard for gaming in the late 80s.

amigacd32.description: The first 32-bit CD-based gaming console released in Europe. Based on the Amiga 1200 architecture, it attempted to position Commodore in the home console market.

amigacdtv.description: A hybrid between an Amiga 500 computer and a CD-ROM player. Designed to be a living room multimedia center before the concept became popular. Precursor to CD-based consoles.

c64.description: The best-selling personal computer of all time. Massive library of games and software. Iconic SID sound chip. Classics like Impossible Mission and The Last Ninja.

c128.description: More powerful successor to the C64 with double the memory and three operating modes, including full C64 compatibility and an advanced CP/M mode.

pet.description: Commodore's first 'all-in-one' computer. With built-in monitor, keyboard, and recorder, it was one of the pioneers of personal computing.

cplus4.description: Productivity-focused computer with ROM-integrated software. It had better graphics and color palette than the C64, but a smaller game library.

c20.description: The predecessor to the Commodore 64 and the first personal computer to sell a million units. Very popular for being affordable and accessible.

msx.description: Home computer standard popular in Japan and Europe. Home to the first entries of Metal Gear. Extensive library of games, many by Konami.

zxspectrum.description: Iconic British computer that popularized gaming in the UK. Massive library of games across all genres. Defined a generation of programmers and players.

zx81.description: Minimalist and extremely affordable computer. With no sound and basic graphics, it was the gateway to programming for thousands of people in the 80s.

amstradcpc.description: Series of 8-bit computers popular in Europe. Built-in monitor and cassette recorder. Excellent game library including arcade ports and exclusive titles.

gx4000.description: Amstrad's attempt to enter the home console market. Based on CPC Plus hardware, it had a short life due to strong 16-bit competition.

dos.description: PC platform that became a leader in gaming. Massive library with classics like Doom, Wolfenstein 3D, Dune II and the entire golden age of adventure games from LucasArts and Sierra.

doom.description: Revolutionary engine that defined modern FPS. Includes classics like Doom, Doom II, Heretic, and Hexen, which laid the foundations for multiplayer and 3D gaming.

scummvm.description: Interpretation engine for classic point-and-click games. Allows you to play graphic adventures from LucasArts, Sierra, Revolution Software, and many others on modern systems.

mame.description: The most complete and ambitious emulator in history. Its goal is to preserve thousands of arcade systems and old computers, allowing almost any arcade game to be played.

fbneo.description: Evolution of FinalBurn Alpha, this emulator specializes in classic arcade systems from Capcom, SNK, and Sega, offering high performance and accuracy.

atomiswave.description: Arcade board based on Dreamcast hardware. It was the home of great fighting titles from SNK and Arc System Works after the end of the Neo Geo.

cps.description: Family of arcade boards developed by Capcom. They dominated arcades for over a decade with legendary titles like Street Fighter II and Final Fight.

cps1.description: The first board in Capcom's CPS series. It popularized beat 'em ups and established the company as an undisputed leader in arcades.

cps2.description: Arcade hardware with the famous QSound sound chip. Home to the Street Fighter Alpha series and the iconic Marvel vs. Capcom crossovers.

cps3.description: The pinnacle of Capcom's 2D animation. Extremely powerful hardware designed to handle massive sprites, masterfully used in Street Fighter III.

arcade.description: Arcade machines that defined the golden age of video games. From Pong and Pac-Man to Street Fighter II and Metal Slug. Specialized hardware for optimal experiences.
